\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:experiments}

\paragraph{Training Data.}
We sample a 132M-token subset of FineWeb~\citep{penedo_2024_fineweb} as the real-data source.
To simulate web-scale synthetic contamination, we generate continuations with Qwen3-0.6B~\citep{yang_2025_qwen3}---the same architecture used for continued pretraining---and inject them at ratio $\rho = 0.4$ via uniform random mixing.
This self-contamination design creates a challenging detection scenario where generator and trainee share the same distribution.

\paragraph{Detector.}
We train a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression classifier on a held-out labeled split, achieving AUC\,=\,0.939 with calibrated ECE\,=\,0.048 after temperature scaling ($T = 0.204$).
The resulting $q$-scores have mean 0.60, standard deviation 0.37, and median 0.71, with 46.3\% of samples in the uncertain range $[0.2, 0.8]$.
We use this lightweight detector rather than neural alternatives (e.g., ModernBERT at AUC\,${\geq}$\,0.98 in \citealt{drayson_2025_detection_collapse}) to test whether score \emph{calibration} matters more than raw discrimination for reweighting.

\paragraph{Training.}
We continue pretraining Qwen3-0.6B from its pretrained weights for 6{,}103 steps (batch size 4, gradient accumulation 4, effective batch 16) with AdamW, cosine schedule (peak lr\,=\,$5{\times}10^{-5}$), max sequence length 2048, and bf16 precision.
All main comparisons use three random seeds (42, 123, 456).

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report held-out perplexity (PPL) on a held-out subset of FineWeb (67.8K documents, $\sim$4M tokens) containing only human-authored text, via sliding-window evaluation (stride 1024).
All evaluations are post-hoc with a unified pipeline; training involves no inline evaluation.

\paragraph{Methods.}
We compare five approaches:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Uniform}: $w_j = 1$ for all $j$ (no contamination handling).
  \item \textbf{Grid-$b$}: fixed $b \in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0\}$, best selected post-hoc by held-out PPL.
        Represents validation-based selection~\citep{drayson_2025_detection_collapse}.
  \item \textbf{ESS-only}: $b^* = \max\{b : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}\}$, the maximum-intervention variant retaining only the stability constraint, ablating $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
  \item \textbf{Golden Ratio}: $w = 1/\varphi \approx 0.618$ for synthetic ($q_j > 0.5$), $w = 1$ otherwise~\citep{he_2025_golden_ratio}.
        Requires known provenance labels (oracle).
  \item \textbf{Adaptive} (ours): per-batch $b^*$ from the dual-constraint formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}), with $\tau = 0.8$ and $n_{\min} = 2$ (half the micro-batch size).
\end{itemize}

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Main Comparison}

Table~\ref{tab:main} reports held-out perplexity across methods and seeds.
Adaptive reweighting achieves mean PPL 17.651, matching grid-best ($b{=}0.5$, mean 17.646) within seed-to-seed variance: the per-seed gap never exceeds 0.007, less than half the cross-seed range of the uniform baseline (17.686--17.702).
This parity comes at zero validation cost---grid search requires $|\mathcal{B}|$ complete training runs (six in our sweep), whereas adaptive requires one.

The grid-$b$ sweep reveals monotonically increasing PPL from $b{=}0.5$ to $b{=}5.0$ (17.651 to 17.818 on seed 42; full sweep in Appendix~\ref{app:grid}), confirming that exponent selection is consequential.
The optimal $b{=}0.5$ differs from the $b{=}10$ reported by \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} at comparable model scale, underscoring the model-dependence of fixed-exponent selection.

ESS-only (maximum intervention) yields mean PPL 17.723 across three seeds, \emph{worse} than uniform (17.694) by 0.029.
Removing $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and maximizing $b$ subject only to $\mathrm{ESS} \geq n_{\min}$ leads to over-downweighting that degrades training, providing direct evidence for the minimum-intervention principle.

The Golden Ratio oracle~\citep{he_2025_golden_ratio} achieves PPL 17.654 on seed 42 using known provenance labels.
Adaptive reaches within 0.001 of this upper bound without provenance access, suggesting the dual constraint recovers near-optimal weights from noisy detector scores alone.

The adaptive $b^*$ distribution (median 0.87, IQR $[0.54, 1.51]$, mean 1.40) confirms that most batches need only moderate intervention.
The constraint regime breakdown in \S\ref{sec:algorithm} shows that $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ prevents over-intervention in the 40\% of reweighted batches where moderate $b$ already meets the quality target.

1	Web corpora increasingly contain machine-generated text.
2	Recent estimates place the synthetic fraction at 20--60\% of crawled data~\citep{cheng_2025_contamination_survey}, and this share grows as language models are deployed for content production at scale.
3	Training on such contaminated data has concrete consequences: \citet{shumailov_2024_model_collapse} show that recursive training on model outputs leads to irreversible quality degradation---\emph{model collapse}---and \citet{dohmatob_2025_strong_collapse} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction suffices to trigger this failure mode, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
4	A central difficulty is that the contamination proportion in any given corpus is unknown: synthetic text enters through diverse, uncoordinated channels with no centralized provenance record.
5	The prevalence, severity, and opacity of synthetic contamination make contamination-aware pretraining a practical necessity.
6	
7	A natural response is \emph{detect-and-reweight}: train a classifier to estimate each sample's synthetic probability $q(x)$, then suppress likely-synthetic samples via the weighting function $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^b$.
8	\citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} demonstrate this approach for model collapse prevention and show that the exponent $b$ critically determines outcomes---their optimal values range from $b{=}10$ for models at ${\leq}360$M parameters to $b{=}1$ at 1.7B, and misspecification degrades results substantially.
9	Selecting $b$ therefore requires per-model validation-set grid search, with computational cost scaling linearly in the number of candidates (six training runs in a typical sweep).
10	Other approaches assume even stronger supervision: \citet{he_2025_golden_ratio} derive theoretically optimal weights from convergence analysis but require the exact contamination ratio $\rho$, which is precisely what is unavailable in practice.
11	Hard detection-and-removal strategies~\citep{feng_2025_beyond_collapse} discard borderline samples entirely, sacrificing the smooth reweighting that continuous $q$-scores enable.
12	
13	Given per-sample detector scores $q(x)$, how should one choose $b$ without a validation set or known contamination proportion?
14	We formulate this as a dual-constrained optimization over each training batch: find the smallest $b$ that ensures the weighted effective real proportion $\aeff(b)$ reaches a quality threshold $\tau$, while keeping Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ above a stability floor $\nmin$.
15	The quality constraint has theoretical grounding: convergence rate under contaminated training improves with the effective real-data fraction~\citep{wang_2026_survive_contamination}, motivating a lower bound on $\aeff$.
16	The stability constraint prevents extreme weight concentration that degrades gradient quality.
17	These two requirements exhibit a natural opposition.
18	$\aeff(b)$ increases monotonically in $b$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}), yielding a lower bound $\btau$---the minimum exponent needed to achieve the target quality.
19	$\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ decreases monotonically, yielding an upper bound $\bess$---the maximum exponent before gradient stability degrades.
20	The adaptive exponent $\bstar = \btau$ when the feasible region $[\btau, \bess]$ is non-empty, embodying a \emph{minimum intervention principle}: apply the least downweighting sufficient to meet the quality target, preserving as much effective training data as possible.
21	When the constraints conflict ($\btau > \bess$), the stability ceiling takes precedence.
22	
23	This minimum-intervention semantics distinguishes the method from the alternative of maximizing $b$ subject only to ESS stability.

Web corpora increasingly contain machine-generated text.
Recent estimates place the synthetic fraction at 20--60\% of crawled data~\citep{cheng_2025_contamination_survey}, and this share grows as language models are deployed for content production at scale.
Training on such contaminated data has concrete consequences: \citet{shumailov_2024_model_collapse} show that recursive training on model outputs leads to irreversible quality degradation---\emph{model collapse}---and \citet{dohmatob_2025_strong_collapse} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction suffices to trigger this failure mode, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
A central difficulty is that the contamination proportion in any given corpus is unknown: synthetic text enters through diverse, uncoordinated channels with no centralized provenance record.
The prevalence, severity, and opacity of synthetic contamination make contamination-aware pretraining a practical necessity.

A natural response is \emph{detect-and-reweight}: train a classifier to estimate each sample's synthetic probability $q(x)$, then suppress likely-synthetic samples via the weighting function $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^b$.
\citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} demonstrate this approach for model collapse prevention and show that the exponent $b$ critically determines outcomes---their optimal values range from $b{=}10$ for models at ${\leq}360$M parameters to $b{=}1$ at 1.7B, and misspecification degrades results substantially.
Selecting $b$ therefore requires per-model validation-set grid search, with computational cost scaling linearly in the number of candidates (six training runs in a typical sweep).
Other approaches assume even stronger supervision: \citet{he_2025_golden_ratio} derive theoretically optimal weights from convergence analysis but require the exact contamination ratio $\rho$, which is precisely what is unavailable in practice.
Hard detection-and-removal strategies~\citep{feng_2025_beyond_collapse} discard borderline samples entirely, sacrificing the smooth reweighting that continuous $q$-scores enable.

Given per-sample detector scores $q(x)$, how should one choose $b$ without a validation set or known contamination proportion?
We formulate this as a dual-constrained optimization over each training batch: find the smallest $b$ that ensures the weighted effective real proportion $\aeff(b)$ reaches a quality threshold $\tau$, while keeping Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ above a stability floor $\nmin$.
The quality constraint has theoretical grounding: convergence rate under contaminated training improves with the effective real-data fraction~\citep{wang_2026_survive_contamination}, motivating a lower bound on $\aeff$.
The stability constraint prevents extreme weight concentration that degrades gradient quality.
These two requirements exhibit a natural opposition.
$\aeff(b)$ increases monotonically in $b$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}), yielding a lower bound $\btau$---the minimum exponent needed to achieve the target quality.
$\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ decreases monotonically, yielding an upper bound $\bess$---the maximum exponent before gradient stability degrades.
The adaptive exponent $\bstar = \btau$ when the feasible region $[\btau, \bess]$ is non-empty, embodying a \emph{minimum intervention principle}: apply the least downweighting sufficient to meet the quality target, preserving as much effective training data as possible.
When the constraints conflict ($\btau > \bess$), the stability ceiling takes precedence.

This minimum-intervention semantics distinguishes the method from the alternative of maximizing $b$ subject only to ESS stability.
Among batches that require reweighting, the dual-constraint solver selects $\bstar$ via the $\aeff$ bound in 40\% of cases, with mean $\bstar{=}1.67$; the ESS-only variant would choose $b{=}4.15$ in these same batches, 2.5$\times$ more aggressive.
The remaining 49.9\% of batches have sufficient real-data content to skip reweighting entirely ($\bstar{=}0$).
The per-batch $\bstar$ distribution (median 0.87, mean 1.40) adapts continuously to each batch's contamination composition without any held-out signal.

The ESS-only variant (maximum intervention) yields mean PPL 17.722---worse than the uniform baseline (17.694)---confirming that maximum intervention degrades training while minimum intervention improves it.
A lightweight TF-IDF + Logistic Regression detector (AUC\,=\,0.939, calibrated ECE\,=\,0.048) suffices throughout, suggesting that score calibration matters more than raw classification accuracy for provenance-based reweighting.

Our contributions:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item A dual-constrained framework for adaptive exponent selection: $\bstar = \inf\{b \geq 0 : \aeff(b) \geq \tau\}$ subject to $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$, computed per-batch from detector scores with minimum-intervention semantics (\S\ref{sec:method}).
\item Empirical evidence that adaptive $\bstar$ matches grid-searched best within seed variance at zero validation cost, and that minimum intervention (dual constraint) outperforms maximum intervention (ESS-only) across three seeds (\S\ref{sec:results}).
\item A demonstration that a lightweight TF-IDF + LR detector with calibrated $q$-scores supports effective reweighting, achieving results comparable to stronger neural detectors (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:experiments}

\paragraph{Training Data.}
We sample a 132M-token subset of FineWeb~\citep{penedo_2024_fineweb} as the real-data source.
To simulate web-scale synthetic contamination, we generate continuations with Qwen3-0.6B~\citep{yang_2025_qwen3}---the same architecture used for continued pretraining---and inject them at ratio $\rho = 0.4$ via uniform random mixing.
This self-contamination design creates a challenging detection scenario where generator and trainee share the same distribution.

\paragraph{Detector.}
We train a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression classifier on a held-out labeled split, achieving AUC\,=\,0.939 with calibrated ECE\,=\,0.048 after temperature scaling ($T = 0.204$).
The resulting $q$-scores have mean 0.60, standard deviation 0.37, and median 0.71, with 46.3\% of samples in the uncertain range $[0.2, 0.8]$.
We use this lightweight detector rather than neural alternatives (e.g., ModernBERT at AUC\,${\geq}$\,0.98 in \citealt{drayson_2025_detection_collapse}) to test whether score \emph{calibration} matters more than raw discrimination for reweighting.

\paragraph{Training.}
We continue pretraining Qwen3-0.6B from its pretrained weights for 6{,}103 steps (batch size 4, gradient accumulation 4, effective batch 16) with AdamW, cosine schedule (peak lr\,=\,$5{\times}10^{-5}$), max sequence length 2048, and bf16 precision.
All main comparisons use three random seeds (42, 123, 456).

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report held-out perplexity (PPL) on a held-out subset of FineWeb (67.8K documents, $\sim$4M tokens) containing only human-authored text, via sliding-window evaluation (stride 1024).
All evaluations are post-hoc with a unified pipeline; training involves no inline evaluation.

\paragraph{Methods.}
We compare five approaches:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Uniform}: $w_j = 1$ for all $j$ (no contamination handling).
  \item \textbf{Grid-$b$}: fixed $b \in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0\}$, best selected post-hoc by held-out PPL.
        Represents validation-based selection~\citep{drayson_2025_detection_collapse}.
  \item \textbf{ESS-only}: $b^* = \max\{b : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}\}$, the maximum-intervention variant retaining only the stability constraint, ablating $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
  \item \textbf{Golden Ratio}: $w = 1/\varphi \approx 0.618$ for synthetic ($q_j > 0.5$), $w = 1$ otherwise~\citep{he_2025_golden_ratio}.
        Requires known provenance labels (oracle).
  \item \textbf{Adaptive} (ours): per-batch $b^*$ from the dual-constraint formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}), with $\tau = 0.8$ and $n_{\min} = 2$ (half the micro-batch size).
\end{itemize}

\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Main Comparison}

Table~\ref{tab:main} reports held-out perplexity across methods and seeds.
Adaptive reweighting achieves mean PPL 17.651, matching grid-best ($b{=}0.5$, mean 17.646) within seed-to-seed variance: the per-seed gap never exceeds 0.007, less than half the cross-seed range of the uniform baseline (17.686--17.702).
This parity comes at zero validation cost---grid search requires $|\mathcal{B}|$ complete training runs (six in our sweep), whereas adaptive requires one.

The grid-$b$ sweep reveals monotonically increasing PPL from $b{=}0.5$ to $b{=}5.0$ (17.651 to 17.818 on seed 42; full sweep in Appendix~\ref{app:grid}), confirming that exponent selection is consequential.
The optimal $b{=}0.5$ differs from the $b{=}10$ reported by \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} at comparable model scale, underscoring the model-dependence of fixed-exponent selection.

ESS-only (maximum intervention) yields mean PPL 17.723 across three seeds, \emph{worse} than uniform (17.694) by 0.029.
Removing $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and maximizing $b$ subject only to $\mathrm{ESS} \geq n_{\min}$ leads to over-downweighting that degrades training, providing direct evidence for the minimum-intervention principle.

The Golden Ratio oracle~\citep{he_2025_golden_ratio} achieves PPL 17.654 on seed 42 using known provenance labels.
Adaptive reaches within 0.001 of this upper bound without provenance access, suggesting the dual constraint recovers near-optimal weights from noisy detector scores alone.

The adaptive $b^*$ distribution (median 0.87, IQR $[0.54, 1.51]$, mean 1.40) confirms that most batches need only moderate intervention.
The constraint regime breakdown in \S\ref{sec:algorithm} shows that $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ prevents over-intervention in the 40\% of reweighted batches where moderate $b$ already meets the quality target.

Web corpora increasingly contain machine-generated text.
Recent estimates place the synthetic fraction at 20--60\% of crawled data~\citep{cheng_2025_contamination_survey}, and this share grows as language models are deployed for content production at scale.
Training on such contaminated data has concrete consequences: \citet{shumailov_2024_model_collapse} show that recursive training on model outputs leads to irreversible quality degradation---\emph{model collapse}---and \citet{dohmatob_2025_strong_collapse} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction suffices to trigger this failure mode, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
A central difficulty is that the contamination proportion in any given corpus is unknown: synthetic text enters through diverse, uncoordinated channels with no centralized provenance record.
The prevalence, severity, and opacity of synthetic contamination make contamination-aware pretraining a practical necessity.

A natural response is \emph{detect-and-reweight}: train a classifier to estimate each sample's synthetic probability $q(x)$, then suppress likely-synthetic samples via the weighting function $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^b$.
\citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} demonstrate this approach for model collapse prevention and show that the exponent $b$ critically determines outcomes---their optimal values range from $b{=}10$ for models at ${\leq}360$M parameters to $b{=}1$ at 1.7B, and misspecification degrades results substantially.
Selecting $b$ therefore requires per-model validation-set grid search, with computational cost scaling linearly in the number of candidates (six training runs in a typical sweep).
Other approaches assume even stronger supervision: \citet{he_2025_golden_ratio} derive theoretically optimal weights from convergence analysis but require the exact contamination ratio $\rho$, which is precisely what is unavailable in practice.
Hard detection-and-removal strategies~\citep{feng_2025_beyond_collapse} discard borderline samples entirely, sacrificing the smooth reweighting that continuous $q$-scores enable.

Given per-sample detector scores $q(x)$, how should one choose $b$ without a validation set or known contamination proportion?
We formulate this as a dual-constrained optimization over each training batch: find the smallest $b$ that ensures the weighted effective real proportion $\aeff(b)$ reaches a quality threshold $\tau$, while keeping Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ above a stability floor $\nmin$.
The quality constraint has theoretical grounding: convergence rate under contaminated training improves with the effective real-data fraction~\citep{wang_2026_survive_contamination}, motivating a lower bound on $\aeff$.
The stability constraint prevents extreme weight concentration that degrades gradient quality.
These two requirements exhibit a natural opposition.
$\aeff(b)$ increases monotonically in $b$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}), yielding a lower bound $\btau$---the minimum exponent needed to achieve the target quality.
$\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ decreases monotonically, yielding an upper bound $\bess$---the maximum exponent before gradient stability degrades.
The adaptive exponent $\bstar = \btau$ when the feasible region $[\btau, \bess]$ is non-empty, embodying a \emph{minimum intervention principle}: apply the least downweighting sufficient to meet the quality target, preserving as much effective training data as possible.
When the constraints conflict ($\btau > \bess$), the stability ceiling takes precedence.

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Synthetic Contamination and Model Collapse.}
Training on recursively generated data leads to irreversible quality degradation---\emph{model collapse}~\citep{shumailov_2024_model_collapse}.
\citet{alemohammad_2024_mad} formalize this as Model Autophagy Disorder, showing that quality or diversity inevitably degrades without fresh real data, even when original training data is retained.
More critically, \citet{dohmatob_2025_strong_collapse} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction (e.g., $1/1000$) suffices to trigger collapse, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
\citet{cheng_2025_contamination_survey} survey the broader contamination landscape, confirming that synthetic content now constitutes an estimated 20--60\% of web corpora.
These results motivate \emph{contamination-aware} training strategies that explicitly account for synthetic provenance rather than treating all tokens equally.

\paragraph{Detection and Filtering of Machine-Generated Text.}
Given the severity of contamination, a natural response is to detect and remove synthetic content.
DetectGPT~\citep{mitchell_2023_detectgpt} performs zero-shot detection via probability curvature, while Min-$k$\% Prob~\citep{shi_2024_minkprob} uses the average log-probability of the lowest-$k$\% tokens as a reference-free signal.
Both produce continuous confidence scores suitable as input to downstream weighting---including ours.
On the mitigation side, \citet{feng_2025_beyond_collapse} prove that even an imperfect verifier prevents collapse, but apply hard binary filtering that discards borderline samples.
\citet{guo_2025_escaping_collapse} similarly rely on verification-based selection.
Hard filtering requires a precision--recall threshold; soft reweighting avoids this trade-off by assigning continuous weights.

Most directly related to our work, \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} propose $w_j = (1{-}q_j)^b$ for collapse prevention via detect-and-reweight, where $q_j$ is the detector's synthetic probability.
We adopt the same weighting formula but differ in several fundamental ways.
\textbf{(i)}~Drayson et al.\ select $b$ via validation-set grid search and fix it throughout training; different model scales require different values ($b{=}10$ for ${\leq}360$M, $b{=}1$ for 1.7B), making the choice \emph{per-model} and expensive.
Our $b^*$ is derived per-batch from dual constraints ($\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}} \geq \tau$, $\mathrm{ESS} \geq n_{\min}$) at zero validation cost.
\textbf{(ii)}~Their SIR resampling discretizes the weight distribution; we apply direct loss reweighting with continuous gradients.
\textbf{(iii)}~They employ a ModernBERT-150M detector (AUC\,=\,0.986) on WikiText-2 (${\sim}$2M tokens); we show that a lightweight TF-IDF+LR detector (AUC\,=\,0.939) suffices on FineWeb-scale data (132M+ tokens), suggesting that score calibration matters more than raw detection accuracy.

\paragraph{Data Mixing and Instance-Level Reweighting.}
A parallel line of work optimizes data composition without targeting synthetic contamination.
At the \emph{domain} level, DoReMi~\citep{xie_2023_doremi} learns mixture weights via Group DRO with a proxy model, DSIR~\citep{xie_2023_dsir} performs importance resampling with $n$-gram features, and \citet{ye_2025_data_mixing_laws} discover predictable functional forms relating mixing ratios to performance.
AIOLI~\citep{chen_2025_aioli} unifies these into an online adaptive framework, while \citet{yang_2026_data_mixing_agent} train an RL agent for domain-weight selection.
These methods do not address instance-level contamination within a domain.
At the \emph{instance} level, SoftDedup~\citep{he_2024_softdedup} downweights high-frequency samples via $n$-gram commonness, \citet{sow_2025_dynamic_reweighting} derive sample weights from per-sample loss with convergence guarantees, and \citet{kuo_2024_data_weighting} show that differentiated weighting of LLM-generated data improves downstream classification.
Our reweighting differs from all of these in being driven by \emph{provenance}---detector scores estimating human vs.\ synthetic origin---rather than loss, frequency, or domain membership.

\paragraph{Theoretical Foundations.}
\citet{he_2025_golden_ratio} derive the optimal real-data weight under known mixture proportions, finding the golden-ratio reciprocal (${\approx}0.62$) optimal when both sources are equally sized.
Their result requires the contamination ratio $k$, unavailable in web-scale settings; we use it as an oracle baseline.
\citet{wang_2026_survive_contamination} prove that contaminated recursive training converges at a rate governed by the effective real-data fraction $\alpha$, providing the theoretical motivation for our quality threshold: ensuring $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) \geq \tau$ guarantees a convergence-rate lower bound.
We operationalize this without the known-proportion assumption, estimating $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ from batch-level statistics online.
For the stability constraint, we build on Kish's effective sample size and the Pareto-smoothed importance sampling framework of \citet{vehtari_2024_psis}.
\citet{kimura_2024_iw_survey} provide a broader treatment of importance weighting under distribution shift, within which our provenance-based reweighting can be viewed as a special case of covariate-shift correction where the covariate is synthetic origin probability.

\paragraph{Synthetic Contamination and Model Collapse.}
Training on recursively generated data leads to irreversible quality degradation---\emph{model collapse}~\citep{shumailov2024model}.
\citet{alemohammad2024mad} formalize this as Model Autophagy Disorder, showing that quality or diversity inevitably degrades without fresh real data, even when original training data is retained.
More critically, \citet{dohmatob2025strong} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction (e.g., $1/1000$) suffices to trigger collapse, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
Independent estimates suggest that synthetic content now constitutes 20--60\% of web corpora, making this threat increasingly urgent.
These results motivate \emph{contamination-aware} training strategies that explicitly account for synthetic provenance rather than treating all tokens equally.

\paragraph{Detection and Filtering of Machine-Generated Text.}
Given the severity of contamination, a natural response is to detect and remove synthetic content.
DetectGPT~\citep{mitchell2023detectgpt} performs zero-shot detection via probability curvature, while Min-$k$\% Prob~\citep{shi2024minkprob} uses the average log-probability of the lowest-$k$\% tokens as a reference-free signal.
Both produce continuous confidence scores suitable as input to reweighting frameworks such as ours.
On the mitigation side, \citet{feng2025beyond} prove that even an imperfect verifier prevents collapse, but apply hard binary filtering that discards borderline samples.
\citet{guo2025escaping} similarly rely on verification-based selection.
Hard filtering requires a precision--recall threshold; soft reweighting avoids this trade-off by assigning continuous weights.

Most directly related to our work, \citet{drayson2025detection} propose $w_j = (1{-}q_j)^b$ for collapse prevention via detect-and-reweight, where $q_j$ is the detector's synthetic probability.

Web pretraining corpora contain an estimated 20--60\% synthetic text whose provenance is unknown at training time.
Existing detect-and-reweight approaches \citep{drayson2025detection} require per-model grid search over the reweighting exponent $b$, costing up to $6{\times}$ the base training budget.

We introduced a dual-constraint framework that derives $\bstar$ per-batch from two batch-level diagnostics: $\aeff(b) \geq \tau$ imposes a quality floor ensuring sufficient real-data gradient signal, while $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$ imposes a stability ceiling preventing weight concentration.
A minimum intervention principle selects $\bstar$ as the smallest exponent satisfying the quality floor, preserving the largest possible effective sample size.
The monotonicity of $\aeff$ (non-decreasing) and $\mathrm{ESS}$ (non-increasing) in $b$ makes this selection tractable via binary search on each batch.

In continued pretraining of Qwen3-0.6B on 132M FineWeb tokens with 40\% synthetic contamination, adaptive $\bstar$ with default hyperparameters ($\tau = 0.8$, $\nmin = 2$) achieves PPL $17.651 {\pm} 0.007$, matching the grid-search-optimal fixed $b$ ($17.646 {\pm} 0.007$) within seed variance and capturing 89.6\% of the grid-best improvement over uniform training ($17.694 {\pm} 0.008$).
It outperforms ESS-only maximum intervention ($17.723 {\pm} 0.006$), confirming that minimum intervention is the better operating point.
A lightweight TF-IDF + logistic regression detector (AUC\,=\,0.939) suffices for effective reweighting, and $\tau \in [0.5, 0.8]$ provides a safe operating range with $\tau = 0.8$ as the recommended default.
The framework eliminates per-model validation grid search entirely.

Our evaluation is limited to a single model scale (0.6B parameters) and a controlled injection setting with known contamination ratio.
The observation that score calibration may matter more than raw discrimination for reweighting effectiveness remains a hypothesis pending controlled comparison across multiple detectors.

Three directions warrant investigation: scaling to larger models (3B+) to test whether $\tau$ and $\nmin$ defaults transfer across scales; controlled comparison across detectors of varying discrimination power (TF-IDF, ModernBERT, neural classifiers) to verify the calibration hypothesis; and evaluation on naturally contaminated web corpora where ground-truth provenance labels are unavailable.

\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:experiments}

\paragraph{Training Data.}
We sample a 132M-token subset of FineWeb~\citep{penedo_2024_fineweb} as the real-data source.
To simulate web-scale synthetic contamination, we generate continuations with Qwen3-0.6B~\citep{yang_2025_qwen3}---the same architecture used for continued pretraining---and inject them at ratio $\rho = 0.4$ via uniform random mixing.
This self-contamination design creates a challenging detection scenario where generator and trainee share the same distribution.

\paragraph{Detector.}
We train a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression classifier on a held-out labeled split, achieving AUC\,=\,0.939 with calibrated ECE\,=\,0.048 after temperature scaling ($T = 0.204$).
The resulting $q$-scores have mean 0.60, standard deviation 0.37, and median 0.71, with 46.3\% of samples in the uncertain range $[0.2, 0.8]$.
We use this lightweight detector rather than neural alternatives (e.g., ModernBERT at AUC\,${\geq}$\,0.98 in \citealt{drayson_2025_detection_collapse}) to test whether score \emph{calibration} matters more than raw discrimination for reweighting.

\paragraph{Training.}
We continue pretraining Qwen3-0.6B from its pretrained weights for 6{,}103 steps (batch size 4, gradient accumulation 4, effective batch 16) with AdamW, cosine schedule (peak lr\,=\,$5{\times}10^{-5}$), max sequence length 2048, and bf16 precision.
All main comparisons use three random seeds (42, 123, 456).

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report held-out perplexity (PPL) on a held-out subset of FineWeb (67.8K documents, $\sim$4M tokens) containing only human-authored text, via sliding-window evaluation (stride 1024).
All evaluations are post-hoc with a unified pipeline; training involves no inline evaluation.

\paragraph{Methods.}
We compare five approaches:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Uniform}: $w_j = 1$ for all $j$ (no contamination handling).
  \item \textbf{Grid-$b$}: fixed $b \in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0\}$, best selected post-hoc by held-out PPL.
        Represents validation-based selection~\citep{drayson_2025_detection_collapse}.
  \item \textbf{ESS-only}: $b^* = \max\{b : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}\}$, the maximum-intervention variant retaining only the stability constraint, ablating $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
  \item \textbf{Golden Ratio}: $w = 1/\varphi \approx 0.618$ for synthetic ($q_j > 0.5$), $w = 1$ otherwise~\citep{he_2025_golden_ratio}.
        Requires known provenance labels (oracle).
  \item \textbf{Adaptive} (ours): per-batch $b^*$ from the dual-constraint formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}), with $\tau = 0.8$ and $n_{\min} = 2$ (half the micro-batch size).
\end{itemize}

Web corpora increasingly contain machine-generated text.
Recent estimates place the synthetic fraction at 20--60\% of crawled data~\citep{cheng_2025_contamination_survey}, and this share grows as language models are deployed for content production at scale.
Training on such contaminated data has concrete consequences: \citet{shumailov_2024_model_collapse} show that recursive training on model outputs leads to irreversible quality degradation---\emph{model collapse}---and \citet{dohmatob_2025_strong_collapse} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction suffices to trigger this failure mode, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
A central difficulty is that the contamination proportion in any given corpus is unknown: synthetic text enters through diverse, uncoordinated channels with no centralized provenance record.
The prevalence, severity, and opacity of synthetic contamination make contamination-aware pretraining a practical necessity.

A natural response is \emph{detect-and-reweight}: train a classifier to estimate each sample's synthetic probability $q(x)$, then suppress likely-synthetic samples via the weighting function $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^b$.
\citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} demonstrate this approach for model collapse prevention and show that the exponent $b$ critically determines outcomes---their optimal values range from $b{=}10$ for models at ${\leq}360$M parameters to $b{=}1$ at 1.7B, and misspecification degrades results substantially.
Selecting $b$ therefore requires per-model validation-set grid search, with computational cost scaling linearly in the number of candidates (six training runs in a typical sweep).
Other approaches assume even stronger supervision: \citet{he_2025_golden_ratio} derive theoretically optimal weights from convergence analysis but require the exact contamination ratio $\rho$, which is precisely what is unavailable in practice.
Hard detection-and-removal strategies~\citep{feng_2025_beyond_collapse} discard borderline samples entirely, sacrificing the smooth reweighting that continuous $q$-scores enable.

Given per-sample detector scores $q(x)$, how should one choose $b$ without a validation set or known contamination proportion?
We formulate this as a dual-constrained optimization over each training batch: find the smallest $b$ that ensures the weighted effective real proportion $\aeff(b)$ reaches a quality threshold $\tau$, while keeping Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ above a stability floor $\nmin$.
The quality constraint has theoretical grounding: convergence rate under contaminated training improves with the effective real-data fraction~\citep{wang_2026_survive_contamination}, motivating a lower bound on $\aeff$.
The stability constraint prevents extreme weight concentration that degrades gradient quality.
These two requirements exhibit a natural opposition.
$\aeff(b)$ increases monotonically in $b$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}), yielding a lower bound $\btau$---the minimum exponent needed to achieve the target quality.
$\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ decreases monotonically, yielding an upper bound $\bess$---the maximum exponent before gradient stability degrades.
The adaptive exponent $\bstar = \btau$ when the feasible region $[\btau, \bess]$ is non-empty, embodying a \emph{minimum intervention principle}: apply the least downweighting sufficient to meet the quality target, preserving as much effective training data as possible.
When the constraints conflict ($\btau > \bess$), the stability ceiling takes precedence.

This minimum-intervention semantics distinguishes the method from the alternative of maximizing $b$ subject only to ESS stability.
Among batches that require reweighting, the dual-constraint solver selects $\bstar$ via the $\aeff$ bound in 40\% of cases, with mean $\bstar{=}1.67$; the ESS-only variant would choose $b{=}4.15$ in these same batches, 2.5$\times$ more aggressive.
The remaining 49.9\% of batches have sufficient real-data content to skip reweighting entirely ($\bstar{=}0$).
The per-batch $\bstar$ distribution (median 0.87, mean 1.40) adapts continuously to each batch's contamination composition without any held-out signal.

On Qwen3-0.6B continued pretraining with 40\% synthetic contamination (132M+ tokens from FineWeb), adaptive reweighting achieves mean held-out perplexity of 17.651 across three seeds, matching the grid-searched optimum ($b{=}0.5$, mean 17.646) within seed-to-seed variance (\S\ref{sec:results}).
The grid sweep requires six complete training runs to identify this optimum; the adaptive method requires one.
The ESS-only variant (maximum intervention) yields mean PPL 17.722---worse than the uniform baseline (17.694)---confirming that maximum intervention degrades training while minimum intervention improves it.
A lightweight TF-IDF + Logistic Regression detector (AUC\,=\,0.939, calibrated ECE\,=\,0.048) suffices throughout, suggesting that score calibration matters more than raw classification accuracy for provenance-based reweighting.

Our contributions:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item A dual-constrained framework for adaptive exponent selection: $\bstar = \inf\{b \geq 0 : \aeff(b) \geq \tau\}$ subject to $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$, computed per-batch from detector scores with minimum-intervention semantics (\S\ref{sec:method}).
\item Empirical evidence that adaptive $\bstar$ matches grid-searched best within seed variance at zero validation cost, and that minimum intervention (dual constraint) outperforms maximum intervention (ESS-only) across three seeds (\S\ref{sec:results}).
\item A demonstration that a lightweight TF-IDF + LR detector with calibrated $q$-scores supports effective reweighting, achieving results comparable to stronger neural detectors (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).
\end{itemize}

A natural mitigation is detect-and-reweight: assign each sample a weight $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^b$ based on a detector's estimated synthetic probability $q(x)$, where larger $b$ downweights suspected synthetic text more aggressively \citep{drayson2025detection}.

Selecting $b$ requires a clean validation set and grid search costing up to $6{\times}$ the base training budget.

The effective real proportion $\aeff(b)$ measures the weighted fraction of gradient signal attributable to real data and imposes a \emph{quality floor}: $\aeff(b) \geq \tau$---at least enough cleaning.

Given the severity of contamination, a natural response is to detect and remove synthetic content.
DetectGPT~\citep{mitchell_2023_detectgpt} performs zero-shot detection via probability curvature, while Min-$k$\% Prob~\citep{shi_2024_minkprob} uses the average log-probability of the lowest-$k$\% tokens as a reference-free signal.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Summary.}
No existing method provides principled per-batch exponent selection without validation.
Our dual-constraint framework fills this gap by deriving the \emph{minimum intervention} $b^*$ from batch-level diagnostics alone, eliminating the per-model grid search of prior work while retaining theoretical grounding in convergence analysis and importance sampling.

\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:experiments}

\paragraph{Training Data.}
We sample a 132M-token subset of FineWeb~\citep{penedo_2024_fineweb} as the real-data source.
To simulate web-scale synthetic contamination, we generate continuations with Qwen3-0.6B~\citep{yang_2025_qwen3}---the same architecture used for continued pretraining---and inject them at ratio $\rho = 0.4$ via uniform random mixing.
This self-contamination design creates a challenging detection scenario where generator and trainee share the same distribution.

\paragraph{Detector.}
We train a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression classifier on a held-out labeled split, achieving AUC\,=\,0.939 with calibrated ECE\,=\,0.048 after temperature scaling ($T = 0.204$).
The resulting $q$-scores have mean 0.60, standard deviation 0.37, and median 0.71, with 46.3\% of samples in the uncertain range $[0.2, 0.8]$.
We use this lightweight detector rather than neural alternatives (e.g., ModernBERT at AUC\,${\geq}$\,0.98 in \citealt{drayson_2025_detection_collapse}) to test whether score \emph{calibration} matters more than raw discrimination for reweighting.

\paragraph{Training.}
We continue pretraining Qwen3-0.6B from its pretrained weights for 6{,}103 steps (batch size 4, gradient accumulation 4, effective batch 16) with AdamW, cosine schedule (peak lr\,=\,$5{\times}10^{-5}$), max sequence length 2048, and bf16 precision.
All main comparisons use three random seeds (42, 123, 456).

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report held-out perplexity (PPL) on a held-out subset of FineWeb (67.8K documents, $\sim$4M tokens) containing only human-authored text, via sliding-window evaluation (stride 1024).
All evaluations are post-hoc with a unified pipeline; training involves no inline evaluation.

\paragraph{Methods.}
We compare five approaches:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Uniform}: $w_j = 1$ for all $j$ (no contamination handling).
  \item \textbf{Grid-$b$}: fixed $b \in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0\}$, best selected post-hoc by held-out PPL.
        Represents validation-based selection~\citep{drayson_2025_detection_collapse}.
  \item \textbf{ESS-only}: $b^* = \max\{b : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}\}$, the maximum-intervention variant retaining only the stability constraint, ablating $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
  \item \textbf{Golden Ratio}: $w = 1/\varphi \approx 0.618$ for synthetic ($q_j > 0.5$), $w = 1$ otherwise~\citep{he_2025_golden_ratio}.
        Requires known provenance labels (oracle).
  \item \textbf{Adaptive} (ours): per-batch $b^*$ from the dual-constraint formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}), with $\tau = 0.8$ and $n_{\min} = 2$ (half the micro-batch size).
\end{itemize}

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Main Comparison}

Table~\ref{tab:main} reports held-out perplexity across methods and seeds.
Adaptive reweighting achieves mean PPL 17.651, matching grid-best ($b{=}0.5$, mean 17.646) within seed-to-seed variance: the per-seed gap never exceeds 0.007, less than half the cross-seed range of the uniform baseline (17.686--17.702).
This parity comes at zero validation cost---grid search requires $|\mathcal{B}|$ complete training runs (six in our sweep), whereas adaptive requires one.

The grid-$b$ sweep reveals monotonically increasing PPL from $b{=}0.5$ to $b{=}5.0$ (17.651 to 17.818 on seed 42; full sweep in Appendix~\ref{app:grid}), confirming that exponent selection is consequential.
The optimal $b{=}0.5$ differs from the $b{=}10$ reported by \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} at comparable model scale, underscoring the model-dependence of fixed-exponent selection.

ESS-only (maximum intervention) yields mean PPL 17.723 across three seeds, \emph{worse} than uniform (17.694) by 0.029.
Removing $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and maximizing $b$ subject only to $\mathrm{ESS} \geq n_{\min}$ leads to over-downweighting that degrades training, providing direct evidence for the minimum-intervention principle.

The Golden Ratio oracle~\citep{he_2025_golden_ratio} achieves PPL 17.654 on seed 42 using known provenance labels.
Adaptive reaches within 0.001 of this upper bound without provenance access, suggesting the dual constraint recovers near-optimal weights from noisy detector scores alone.

The adaptive $b^*$ distribution (median 0.87, IQR $[0.54, 1.51]$, mean 1.40) confirms that most batches need only moderate intervention.
The constraint regime breakdown in \S\ref{sec:algorithm} shows that $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ prevents over-intervention in the 40\% of reweighted batches where moderate $b$ already meets the quality target.

\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Seed 42} & \textbf{Seed 123} & \textbf{Seed 456} & \textbf{Mean} \\
\midrule

ESS-only               & 17.730 & 17.720 & 17.719 & 17.723 \\
Golden Ratio$^\dagger$ & 17.654 & --     & --     & --     \\
\midrule
Adaptive (ours)        & 17.653 & 17.643 & 17.657 & 17.651 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Held-out perplexity (PPL, $\downarrow$).
Grid-best selects the optimal fixed $b$ post-hoc from six candidates.
$^\dagger$Evaluated on seed 42 only.
Best per column in \textbf{bold}.}
\label{tab:main}
\end{table}

\subsection{Sensitivity Analysis}

\paragraph{Quality threshold $\tau$.}
Table~\ref{tab:tau} varies $\tau$ while holding $n_{\min} = 2$ (seed 42).
All values in $\tau \in [0.5, 0.8]$ improve over uniform, with $\tau = 0.8$ achieving the lowest PPL (17.653).
Higher $\tau$ demands greater $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$, forcing the solver to increase $b^*$: mean $\bar{b}^*$ rises monotonically from 0.39 at $\tau{=}0.5$ to 3.08 at $\tau{=}0.95$.
Below 0.8, reweighting is too gentle to fully exploit the detector signal; above, $b^*$ inflates past diminishing returns and PPL degrades.
The range $[0.5, 0.8]$ provides a wide safe operating region, with $\tau = 0.8$ as the recommended default.

\caption{Sensitivity to $\tau$ (seed 42, $n_{\min}{=}2$, $\rho{=}0.4$).
$\Delta_{\mathrm{unif}}$: PPL change vs.\ uniform baseline (17.694).

\label{tab:tau}

\paragraph{Minimum ESS $n_{\min}$.}
Removing the ESS floor ($n_{\min} = 1$) allows $b^*$ to inflate to mean 7.20, degrading PPL to 17.789---0.095 worse than uniform.
At $n_{\min} = 2$ ($= \lfloor B/2 \rfloor$ for batch size $B{=}4$), PPL stabilizes at 17.653; $n_{\min} = 3$ yields a comparable 17.644.
The coupling $n_{\min} = \lfloor B/2 \rfloor$ provides a configuration-aware default that balances reweighting headroom against gradient stability.

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Synthetic Contamination and Model Collapse.}
Training on recursively generated data leads to irreversible quality degradation---\emph{model collapse}~\citep{shumailov_2024_model_collapse}.
\citet{alemohammad_2024_mad} formalize this as Model Autophagy Disorder, showing that quality or diversity inevitably degrades without fresh real data, even when original training data is retained.
More critically, \citet{dohmatob_2025_strong_collapse} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction (e.g., $1/1000$) suffices to trigger collapse, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
\citet{cheng_2025_contamination_survey} survey the broader contamination landscape, confirming that synthetic content now constitutes an estimated 20--60\% of web corpora.
These results motivate \emph{contamination-aware} training strategies that explicitly account for synthetic provenance rather than treating all tokens equally.

\paragraph{Detection and Filtering of Machine-Generated Text.}
Given the severity of contamination, a natural response is to detect and remove synthetic content.
DetectGPT~\citep{mitchell_2023_detectgpt} performs zero-shot detection via probability curvature, while Min-$k$\% Prob~\citep{shi_2024_minkprob} uses the average log-probability of the lowest-$k$\% tokens as a reference-free signal.
Both produce continuous confidence scores suitable as input to downstream weighting---including ours.
On the mitigation side, \citet{feng_2025_beyond_collapse} prove that even an imperfect verifier prevents collapse, but apply hard binary filtering that discards borderline samples.
\citet{guo_2025_escaping_collapse} similarly rely on verification-based selection.
Hard filtering requires a precision--recall threshold; soft reweighting avoids this trade-off by assigning continuous weights.

Most directly related to our work, \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} propose $w_j = (1{-}q_j)^b$ for collapse prevention via detect-and-reweight, where $q_j$ is the detector's synthetic probability.
We adopt the same weighting formula but differ in several fundamental ways.
\textbf{(i)}~Drayson et al.\ select $b$ via validation-set grid search and fix it throughout training; different model scales require different values ($b{=}10$ for ${\leq}360$M, $b{=}1$ for 1.7B), making the choice \emph{per-model} and expensive.
Our $b^*$ is derived per-batch from dual constraints ($\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}} \geq \tau$, $\mathrm{ESS} \geq n_{\min}$) at zero validation cost.
\textbf{(ii)}~Their SIR resampling discretizes the weight distribution; we apply direct loss reweighting with continuous gradients.
\textbf{(iii)}~They employ a ModernBERT-150M detector (AUC\,=\,0.986) on WikiText-2 (${\sim}$2M tokens); we show that a lightweight TF-IDF+LR detector (AUC\,=\,0.939) suffices on FineWeb-scale data (132M+ tokens), suggesting that score calibration matters more than raw detection accuracy.

\paragraph{Data Mixing and Instance-Level Reweighting.}
A parallel line of work optimizes data composition without targeting synthetic contamination.
At the \emph{domain} level, DoReMi~\citep{xie_2023_doremi} learns mixture weights via Group DRO with a proxy model, DSIR~\citep{xie_2023_dsir} performs importance resampling with $n$-gram features, and \citet{ye_2025_data_mixing_laws} discover predictable functional forms relating mixing ratios to performance.
AIOLI~\citep{chen_2025_aioli} unifies these into an online adaptive framework, while \citet{yang_2026_data_mixing_agent} train an RL agent for domain-weight selection.
These methods do not address instance-level contamination within a domain.
At the \emph{instance} level, SoftDedup~\citep{he_2024_softdedup} downweights high-frequency samples via $n$-gram commonness, \citet{sow_2025_dynamic_reweighting} derive sample weights from per-sample loss with convergence guarantees, and \citet{kuo_2024_data_weighting} show that differentiated weighting of LLM-generated data improves downstream classification.
Our reweighting differs from all of these in being driven by \emph{provenance}---detector scores estimating human vs.\ synthetic origin---rather than loss, frequency, or domain membership.

\paragraph{Theoretical Foundations.}
\citet{he_2025_golden_ratio} derive the optimal real-data weight under known mixture proportions, finding the golden-ratio reciprocal (${\approx}0.62$) optimal when both sources are equally sized.
Their result requires the contamination ratio $k$, unavailable in web-scale settings; we use it as an oracle baseline.
\citet{wang_2026_survive_contamination} prove that contaminated recursive training converges at a rate governed by the effective real-data fraction $\alpha$, providing the theoretical motivation for our quality threshold: ensuring $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) \geq \tau$ guarantees a convergence-rate lower bound.
We operationalize this without the known-proportion assumption, estimating $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ from batch-level statistics online.
For the stability constraint, we build on Kish's effective sample size and the Pareto-smoothed importance sampling framework of \citet{vehtari_2024_psis}.
\citet{kimura_2024_iw_survey} provide a broader treatment of importance weighting under distribution shift, within which our provenance-based reweighting can be viewed as a special case of covariate-shift correction where the covariate is synthetic origin probability.

Training on recursively generated data leads to irreversible quality degradation---\emph{model collapse}~\citep{shumailov_2024_model_collapse}.
\citet{alemohammad_2024_mad} formalize this as Model Autophagy Disorder, showing that quality or diversity inevitably degrades without fresh real data, even when original training data is retained.

We introduced Minimum Intervention Reweighting, a dual-constrained framework for contamination-aware pretraining that selects per-batch exponents $b^*$ without validation data.
The method finds the smallest $b$ satisfying $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) \geq \tau$ subject to $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}$, enforcing a minimum-intervention principle: apply only as much downweighting as needed to meet a quality floor, no more.
This stands in direct contrast to ESS-only (maximum-intervention) strategies, which we show degrade performance below even uniform baselines by over-downweighting contaminated samples.

Across three seeds at 0.6B scale with 40\% synthetic contamination, adaptive $b^*$ matches grid-search-optimal PPL (17.651 vs.\ 17.646) within seed variance, eliminating the $|\mathcal{B}|$-run grid search entirely.
The quality threshold $\tau$ is robust across $[0.5, 0.8]$---all values in this range outperform uniform weighting.
A lightweight TF-IDF + logistic regression detector (AUC\,0.94) suffices when post-hoc calibrated (ECE\,0.048); score calibration matters more than raw discriminative power.
The batch-level constraint regime---49.9\% clean (no reweighting needed), 20.2\% $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$-binding, 30.0\% ESS-binding---confirms that both constraints are active and complementary in practice.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Scale.}
All experiments use a single model size (Qwen3-0.6B) with batch size 4.
Batch-level $q$-score statistics concentrate differently at larger batch sizes typical of 3B+ training; the optimal $\tau$ range and constraint dynamics may shift at scale.

\paragraph{Contamination distribution.}
We inject synthetic data via uniform random mixing at a controlled ratio ($\rho{=}0.4$).
Real web-scale contamination is domain-skewed, which may alter within-batch $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ distributions and require domain-aware extensions.

\paragraph{Detector coverage.}
We evaluate one detector family (TF-IDF + logistic regression).
Although our results suggest calibration dominates discrimination for reweighting quality, a systematic ablation across detector architectures and quality levels is needed.

\paragraph{Threshold.}
$\tau$ is an empirical hyperparameter.
The convergence theory of \citet{wang_2026_survive_contamination} assumes a known contamination proportion $\alpha$, which we do not require; bridging this gap to derive $\tau$ from first principles remains open.

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report held-out perplexity only.
Downstream task evaluation (MMLU, HellaSwag) would strengthen the practical case, particularly at scales where PPL differences translate more reliably to task performance.

\paragraph{Effect size.}
The PPL improvement over uniform weighting is 0.043 at 0.6B/40\% contamination.
While consistent across seeds, this effect is modest; we expect amplification at higher contamination ratios and larger model scales, but verification is ongoing.
